Offshore Wind’s Real Test Is a Repeatable Maritime Construction Sequence

U.S. offshore wind’s most visible problems are federal policy reversals, expensive capital, uneconomic power contracts and turbine failures. Those factors determine whether a project survives long enough to enter construction. They remain the industry’s dominant upstream risks.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-06-23 · 15 min read

In brief

  • 330+ vessels | Three U.S. projects still depended on specialized foreign installation assets.
  • 46 of 50 | U.S.-yard vessel investments were support vessels, not installation assets.
  • Early 2027 | Charybdis remains committed to Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind.
  • 2027 | Empire Wind will test Maersk Viridis and the feeder-barge model at scale.
  • Two campaigns | Successive charters, not another vessel launch, would signal a durable market.

The visible problems come before the maritime gate

Projects that clear those gates encounter a different constraint. They must assemble a legally usable combination of installation vessels, feeder barges, cable and rock-placement assets, ports, crews and weather windows. These components must be available in the correct sequence, not merely somewhere in the global fleet.

The maritime calendar is therefore a project-level sequential gate, not a singular national shortage. A vessel can exist and still be unavailable, incompatible, committed elsewhere or legally unable to move a particular cargo. A port can be complete and still lack an anchor project. A financed wind farm can lose a construction season if a stop-work order causes its vessel spread to demobilize.

The central commercialization question is whether the United States can progress from isolated, project-specific solutions to repeatable procurement across successive projects.

The constraint is an installation spread, not a ship count

The Government Accountability Office reviewed Vineyard Wind, Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind and Revolution Wind—three projects under construction as of August 2025. Together they used more than 330 unique vessels, about 80% of them U.S.-flagged. The domestic maritime contribution was substantial, but it was concentrated in crew transport, towing, surveying, barges and other support functions. Specialized foreign vessels still performed many installation tasks. (GAO offshore-wind vessel report)

As of June 2025, GAO found no Jones Act-compliant vessel in the U.S. fleet capable of installing turbines and turbine components. Two developers instead used U.S.-flagged feeder barges to transport components from domestic ports to foreign wind-turbine installation vessels stationed offshore. That zero count is now historical: Charybdis began installing turbines in January 2026. But the feeder model remains important because it proves that domestic WTIV scarcity can be routed around.

The Jones Act shapes the physical construction method because coastwise transportation of merchandise generally requires a qualified U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-documented vessel with predominantly U.S. crewing. Offshore projects add operational complexity: cargo classification, the loading point, installed foundations, scour protection and the legal status of the offshore location can all affect the ruling. CBP decisions are transaction-specific; not every offshore operation automatically requires a Jones Act-qualified vessel.

This is why the meaningful unit of capacity is the entire installation spread. A project needs the turbine vessel or feeder system, compatible components, a marshaling port, qualified crews, tugs, cable and rock-installation assets, regulatory documentation and workable weather at the same time.

Two national studies show the scale, but their figures should not be conflated. A March 2022 demand study estimated that a 30 GW buildout would require at least 2,100 turbines and foundations, 6,800 miles of cable, five to six WTIVs, 10 feeder barges and four cable-lay vessels. A separate January 2023 road-map scenario estimated $22.4 billion of manufacturing, port and vessel investment and used somewhat different vessel ranges. (DOE and NREL supply-chain road map)

The named projects show partial relief, not a scalable system

Charybdis is the clearest evidence that physical capacity is improving. Dominion Energy built the 472-foot vessel at Seatrium’s AmFELS yard in Brownsville, Texas. Dominion reported more than 14,000 tons of domestic steel and more than 1,200 workers at peak construction. The vessel can carry component sets for four turbines and is designed for turbines rated at 12 MW or more. (Dominion on Charybdis)

Its first campaign is Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind, a 2.6 GW project with 176 turbines rated at approximately 14.7 MW each. Charybdis installed the first commercial turbine in January 2026, and CVOW exported its first electricity on March 23. Dominion expects the vessel to remain committed through project completion in early 2027. (CVOW project timeline)

That is real relief, but it is concentrated in one vertically integrated project. Dominion owns both the wind project and the vessel, allowing the initial workload and utilization risk to remain within one corporate system. The arrangement does not yet prove that an independent owner could finance the same asset against a competitive sequence of third-party charters.

Empire Wind will test a different model. Its 54 monopile foundations and offshore substation were installed before turbine installation, while the project’s purpose-built WTIV, Maersk Viridis, was delivered by Seatrium on February 26, 2026. The vessel is expected to work with U.S.-flag feeder assets rather than transport turbine components directly from a U.S. port. Empire Wind identifies 2027 as its commercial-operation year. (Empire Wind project)

Maersk Viridis also illustrates how tightly vessel economics depend on project timing. Maersk previously terminated its $475 million shipbuilding contract when the vessel was 98.9% complete. The parties later settled the dispute, including a $360 million remaining balance and a $250 million credit arrangement. Delivery resolved the construction dispute; the operational question is now whether the vessel and feeder spread execute Empire Wind predictably and obtain follow-on work. (Reuters on the settlement)

Revolution Wind is particularly important as counterevidence. The project was about 80% complete, with 45 of 65 turbines installed, when federal authorities halted work in August 2025. It later restarted, exceeded 90% completion and began delivering electricity in March 2026. The interruption threatened a live construction sequence, but it did not permanently destroy it. (Revolution Wind project update)

Vineyard Wind shows the opposite handoff. Its July 2024 blade failure led regulators to approve blade-removal work covering as many as 22 turbines. Once turbine quality and OEM support became the binding problem, vessel availability could not restore normal operation by itself. (BOEM on Vineyard Wind 1)

Financing determines whether capacity becomes a market

GAO identified 50 offshore-wind vessels that had been delivered, were under construction or were on order at U.S. shipyards as of August 2025. Forty-six were support vessels; only four were installation-specific investments or potential investments. That mix reflects bankability, not merely engineering difficulty.

Crew-transfer vessels and service-operation vessels can work through commissioning and then support an operating wind farm for years. Owners told GAO that CTV and SOV charters can extend as long as 15 years. One developer reported spending more than $216 million on 13 CTVs and $194 million on one SOV. Long contracts give lenders a revenue stream against which debt can be amortized.

Installation vessels operate differently. They perform discrete campaigns and need a credible sequence of future projects. A vessel designed for one turbine generation may also become less useful as turbine dimensions change. A shipowner therefore needs visibility beyond a single project, while a developer is reluctant to reserve an expensive vessel before permits, financing and component schedules are secure.

Public finance has not closed this gap. Four offshore-wind vessel applications covering seven vessels and more than $584 million received no MARAD-backed financing as of GAO’s review. All seven vessels were ultimately built using private finance. MARAD described a best-case review period of six to nine months, while one applicant reported a process lasting more than two years. (GAO financing findings)

The result is a circular dependency. Developers need vessels before they can build. Vessel owners need multiple credible projects before they can finance. Shipyards need repeat orders before they invest in facilities and workforce learning. Ports need anchor tenants before public infrastructure becomes commercially productive.

The binding event is therefore not another launch ceremony. It is a contract that links two or more successive projects to the same installation ecosystem.

The next value pools sit around utilization and risk

The largest disclosed capital figures do not automatically identify where durable value will accrue. A $700 million-class vessel can absorb steel, imported equipment, financing costs and yard overruns without producing attractive returns for its owner or builder. A publicly funded port can become stranded infrastructure if it never secures a second tenant.

More defensible revenue lies where contracts provide duration or where one party is paid to bear schedule risk. CTV and SOV owners can secure operating-life charters. Cable, trenching and rock-installation contractors can gain work as the critical path moves beyond turbine erection. Port operators can convert project-specific construction into recurring berth, storage, crane and handling revenue—but only if multiple users arrive.

Great Lakes Dredge & Dock’s Acadia illustrates both the opportunity and the limitation. The $197 million vessel was delivered in June 2026 for subsea rock installation. Its disclosed sequence includes Empire Wind and Sunrise Wind, followed by European work covering much of 2027. The vessel adds U.S.-built capability, but its international deployment also signals that the domestic pipeline cannot yet provide continuous employment. (Great Lakes on Acadia delivery)

Cable work could become the next control point. The planned Kalypso U.S.-flag cable-lay vessel was cancelled after developer negotiations ended amid permitting and market uncertainty. By contrast, Crowley and Nexans assigned the Louisiana-built Marmac 306 barge to Empire Wind’s export-cable work. These cases suggest that capacity may expand through a mixture of purpose-built vessels, converted barges and foreign specialist assets rather than a single domestic fleet model.

Ports face the same commercialization test. Portsmouth Marine Terminal is actively staging CVOW components. South Brooklyn Marine Terminal supports Empire Wind’s New York logistics. The New Jersey Wind Port was conceived as a more than 200-acre purpose-built marshaling facility. Their strategic value depends on repeat throughput, not sunk construction expenditure.

Public-company exposure sits across this chain. Dominion controls Charybdis and its anchor workload. Equinor coordinates Empire Wind, Maersk Viridis and South Brooklyn logistics. Ørsted and its partners have experienced the cost of interrupting Revolution Wind’s construction sequence. Seatrium bears shipyard and credit exposure. Great Lakes Dredge & Dock depends on geographically diversified utilization for Acadia. GE Vernova’s Vineyard Wind dispute demonstrates how OEM reliability can displace the maritime bottleneck entirely. These are operating exposures, not investment recommendations.

The closest base rate is a decade of workarounds

This problem did not first appear in 2026. GAO’s 2020 offshore-wind vessel report was already examining Jones Act constraints and alternative vessel strategies. Six years later, the first projects had created substantial U.S.-flag support activity, but turbine installation still relied on foreign vessels and feeder systems until Charybdis entered service. (GAO 2020 vessel report)

The closest international comparison is Europe’s gradual buildout of specialized offshore-wind fleets. Europe created deeper project sequencing over decades, allowing owners to move vessels between nearby markets as turbines increased in size. The similarity is the recurring danger of technical obsolescence and cyclical overbuilding. The difference is that the U.S. has a thinner, more policy-sensitive project pipeline and an additional coastwise-transport constraint.

The historical lesson is not that the United States must reproduce Europe’s fleet vessel for vessel. It is that specialized maritime assets become financeable when owners can see repeated workloads. Without that visibility, the market alternates between scarcity during construction windows and idle steel after projects disappear.

Relief is therefore uneven. Domestic turbine-installation capacity is no longer zero, but Charybdis remains occupied through early 2027. Maersk Viridis adds capable global capacity and has an Empire Wind assignment, but it does not provide Jones Act-qualified component transport. Acadia broadens the stack into rock placement, then leaves for European work. A system-level easing would require these assets—or substitutes—moving directly into successive U.S. campaigns.

The strongest counterargument is that demand may disappear

The maritime thesis fails if too few projects survive upstream policy and economic gates. In that scenario, vessels are not scarce; they are underutilized.

Lease cancellations, stop-work orders, weak offtake economics and turbine failures can shrink the post-2027 construction pipeline before owners commit to another generation of specialized vessels. Acadia’s planned European utilization is consistent with this interpretation. The absence of an announced successor campaign for Charybdis may also reflect insufficient demand rather than a capacity bottleneck.

Foreign WTIVs and feeder barges offer another challenge to domestic scarcity claims. Two projects have already demonstrated that the model can work legally and physically. If Maersk Viridis installs Empire Wind’s turbines with reliable feeder cycles, manageable standby and competitive cost, developers may have little reason to finance several expensive Jones Act WTIVs.

The proposed migration into software, compliance services and risk-transfer products is also unproven. Projects clearly need weather forecasting, AIS data, port inventory control, lift planning and coastwise documentation. But the available evidence does not identify a dominant commercial platform, proprietary data owner or recurring third-party software margin.

What remains defensible is narrower: advanced projects face a dated coordination problem, and the market has not demonstrated that it can procure the necessary spread repeatedly without bespoke ownership, legal or financing structures.

What would turn isolated relief into a system

A repeatable market would have visible characteristics. Charybdis or another WTIV would move directly from one project to a second. A developer would reserve capacity across multiple construction seasons. A feeder system would be reused without a new legal architecture for every campaign. Ports would secure second anchor tenants. Lenders or MARAD would close financing against portfolio charters rather than a single sponsor-owned project.

The thesis would weaken if CVOW and Empire Wind finish within their stated windows with predictable installation rates and limited standby losses, yet no additional vessels are ordered because future project demand remains structurally inadequate. That outcome would show that the main problem is not maritime capacity but the absence of projects worth serving.

It would strengthen if a fully permitted and financed project loses a construction season because the required vessel–port–crew spread cannot be assembled. The distinction matters: one outcome points to demand destruction; the other to a genuine execution bottleneck.

What to watch

  • September 30, 2026 | Empire Wind confirms its first turbine installed by the Maersk Viridis spread.
  • March 31, 2027 | Dominion announces completion of CVOW’s offshore construction campaign.
  • June 30, 2027 | Dominion discloses Charybdis’s successor charter or non-wind deployment.
  • December 31, 2027 | Empire Wind reaches formal commercial operation.
  • December 31, 2027 | Acadia begins its contracted European offshore-energy work.
  • December 31, 2029 | A financed U.S. series order for at least two installation vessels reaches FID.

The decisive milestone is a second campaign

U.S. offshore wind now has operating domestic installation capacity, a delivered next-generation foreign WTIV, functioning feeder-system precedents and new rock-placement capability. The industry has moved beyond the claim that no physical solution exists.

It has not yet shown that those solutions form a market. The decisive evidence will be a second campaign: the same vessel, port, feeder structure or financing model moving from one project into another with limited idle time and no extraordinary intervention.

Until that happens, the maritime construction calendar remains a consequential but conditional gate. It becomes binding only after a project survives policy, offtake, financing and turbine risk—and precisely because the project has survived them.
